output.title: When a rollback drill is worth the time
output.body:
If you run one recurring workflow in a small business, a rollback drill is not a philosophy exercise. It is a simple decision about whether you can undo a change before it creates manual cleanup.

For an owner-operator, the rule of thumb is straightforward: if the workflow touches money, customer data, or another repeatable multi-step process, write down the rollback steps before the next change goes live. If it is a low-stakes process that is easy to rebuild by hand, do not spend time on a drill just because it sounds disciplined.

That keeps the question bounded. You are not trying to prepare for every possible failure. You are checking whether one failure would be annoying or expensive enough that a small rehearsal pays for itself in time and attention.

A practical next step is to pick the next change, write the fallback steps in plain English, and test them once in a quiet window. Then note where the handoff breaks, where approval is needed, and whether a human still has to sign off before money moves.

The point is not elegance. It is knowing whether your backup plan exists on paper or only in your head.
